title: Governor of Vermont

context.text: Incumbent Republican Phil Scott is seeking a sixth two-year term. He was unopposed in the August 11, 2026 Republican primary.
Economist Amanda Janoo, a first-time candidate, won the August 11, 2026 Democratic primary over Aly Richards, former head of Let's Grow Kids, and also holds the Progressive Party line.

Three other candidates are on the printed ballot: June Goodband (Peace and Justice), Dean Roy (Freedom and Unity) and Brian Judd (independent). Constitution Party write-in Mark Grimek and write-ins David King and Bryan Ponnwitz have also declared; they are not profiled here.

candidates.name: Phil Scott
candidates.ballotNote: Seeking a sixth term; unopposed in the Republican primary.

summary.text: Phil Scott is the Republican Governor of Vermont, first elected in 2016. A longtime business owner from Barre, he served in the state Senate (2001–2011) and as lieutenant governor (2011–2017). In 2026 he vetoed bills on reference-based health-care pricing, energy facilities, school mental-health programs and union organizing among Department of Corrections employees, and signed H.955, on next steps in transforming Vermont's education system.

background.text: Born in Barre, Vermont; B.S. from the University of Vermont; long-time business owner who set records at Thunder Road speedbowl.
Served in the Vermont Senate (Washington district) 2001–2011 and as the 81st lieutenant governor 2011–2017.
Elected governor in 2016 and re-elected four times since.

priorities.text: Making Vermont affordable and growing the tax base; describes his approach as pragmatic and incremental.
priorities.quote: We need to take care of what's before us. I'm willing to compromise, I'm willing to work together, but it's got to make sense for the average Vermonter

priorities.text: Says he would propose a package of tax cuts or credits; says he would prefer not to raise taxes.
priorities.quote: I would prefer not to raise any taxes

positions.summary: Opposes Janoo's proposed income surcharge on high earners, arguing wealthy residents would leave.
positions.quote: You're raising a tax on a group that I don't think will pay it.

record.text: Vetoed S.190 (reference-based pricing and the Green Mountain Care Board) on June 16, 2026, saying the bill would exclude most payers from affordability gains and that a veto means the Green Mountain Care Board's 2027 hospital revenue reductions apply to all Vermonters paying for insurance.

Vetoed H.710 (defining electricity generating facilities) and H.817 (mental health literacy and peer-to-peer supports in schools) on June 17, 2026; on H.817, which required the Department of Mental Health to make a proposal in its fiscal year 2028 budget for funding such programming, he called it "a clear separation of powers violation."
Vetoed S.230 (fair employment practices) on June 18, 2026, saying it favored one union over another in Department of Corrections organizing.
Signed H.955, "An act relating to next steps in transforming Vermont's education system," and S.328 (housing and common interest communities) on June 18, 2026.

candidates.researchNotes: Positions are limited to what could be directly sourced; his campaign website was not loaded.

candidates.name: Amanda Janoo
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 2026 Democratic primary; also the Progressive Party candidate.

summary.text: Amanda Janoo is a first-time candidate and economist who has worked in economic development for the United Nations and with the Wellbeing Economy Alliance. She proposes higher taxes on top earners, second homes and large tech companies' digital advertising revenue; she says the income surcharge would fund free primary and preventive health care and second-home revenue would reduce property taxes.

background.text: Political newcomer; has worked in economic development for the United Nations and in economic sustainability with the Wellbeing Economy Alliance.
Won the Democratic nomination in August 2026.

priorities.text: Raising revenue from high earners, second homes and large digital advertisers to fund free primary and preventive care and lower property taxes.
priorities.quote: Taxes are one of the levers, or tools, that we can utilize as a way to achieve that.

priorities.text: Program implementation and evaluation to determine what works.
priorities.quote: I've spent my career working in the executive branch of government

positions.summary: Proposes a 2% surcharge on personal income over $250,000 and an 8% surcharge over $500,000, a higher tax rate on certain housing she calls extractive (including luxury second homes, commercial vacation rentals and vacant investment properties), and a tax on large tech companies' digital advertising revenue.
positions.quote: This plan will be funded through our Fair Share Tax Proposal, which asks the wealthiest Vermonters to contribute the equivalent cuts from the Big Beautiful Bill.

positions.summary: Would use surcharge revenue to fund free primary and preventive care for all Vermonters.
positions.quote: Guarantee free primary and preventive healthcare for every Vermonter by eliminating copays, deductibles, and insurance barriers, making primary care the front door to a future universal healthcare system.

candidates.researchNotes: Positions and statements come from her campaign platform page (janooforvt.com/platform-page) and VTDigger coverage. Her platform lists 'reproductive freedom' only within a list of rights, so no abortion statement is shown. Not found in her own words: rent regulation (news outlets report she would let towns adopt rent control, but no first-person quote was located), guns, minimum wage, immigration enforcement.

statements.quote: Support locally driven housing solutions by simplifying permitting for permanently affordable housing, adaptive reuse projects, accessory dwelling units, and small-scale infill while preserving strong environmental protections and giving towns greater flexibility to meet local housing needs.
statements.context: On her campaign website platform page

statements.quote: Create childcare and early-learning hubs in underused school space by helping schools partner with local childcare providers.
statements.context: On her campaign website platform page, community schools section

candidates.name: June Goodband
candidates.ballotNote: Peace and Justice Party candidate; also ran for governor in 2024.

summary.text: June Goodband is the Peace and Justice Party candidate for governor and was the party's 2024 nominee. A reference listing describes her as a psychotherapist and progressive activist.

priorities.text: Tax policy: progressive taxation in place of homestead taxes to pay for education, with higher taxes on high incomes and on vacant buildings that could be used for housing.
priorities.quote: Increase taxes on high incomes and buildings that could be used for housing but are left vacant for most of the year.

priorities.text: Universal health care by implementing Vermont's law to reduce costs and increase access.

positions.summary: Campaign site calls for increasing taxes on high incomes.
positions.quote: Increase taxes on high incomes and buildings that could be used for housing but are left vacant for most of the year.

positions.summary: Campaign site lists universal health care among her priorities and calls for implementing Vermont's law.
positions.quote: Universal Health Care Implement Vermont's law to reduce costs, increase access. and improve outcomes.

candidates.researchNotes: Positions and statements come from her campaign website only (june4govvt.org); no news interviews were found. Her 'living wage' line is not shown as a minimum-wage statement. Not found: abortion, guns, immigration, school choice.

statements.quote: Make it easier to build modest housing and more difficult to build luxury housing.

candidates.name: Brian Judd

summary.text: Brian Judd is an independent candidate for governor. A reference listing describes him as an actor and Navy veteran who ran for city council in 2021 and the state House in 2022.

priorities.text: Says his first executive order would seek the "complete and total repeal" of Act 181, Vermont's 2024 land-use and housing law, per a Vermont Daily Chronicle report on his campaign statement.

candidates.researchNotes: No campaign website found. The only account of his platform is a Vermont Daily Chronicle report (Aug. 24, 2026) summarizing a campaign statement; it contains one short direct quote and no stated position on the guide's issues, so no positions or statements were added. The report's paraphrased list of other priorities (taxes, psychiatric hospitals, audits) is omitted because no quote from him accompanies it.

candidates.name: Dean Roy

summary.text: Dean Roy is the Freedom and Unity Party candidate for governor, a party he created. The Associated Press (via Fortune) described him in March 2026 as a freshman at Stowe High School and the first candidate for governor under age 18 on Vermont's general-election ballot.

priorities.text: No new restrictions on personal freedom: Roy promises no new restrictions on any freedoms.
priorities.quote: Roy promises no new restrictions on any freedoms.

priorities.text: Public option for health coverage, with an eventual move to universal healthcare.
priorities.quote: Dean supports an eventual move to universal healthcare.

priorities.text: Affordable housing: build homes for under $150,000.
priorities.quote: Roy is committed to building affordable units, with the aim being to build houses for under 150k

priorities.text: Statewide ban on Flock cameras and protecting the privacy of Vermonters.
priorities.quote: Dean supports a statewide ban on Flock cameras, and will make protecting privacy of all Vermonters a very high priority.

positions.summary: Campaign platform page says the right to abortion will be protected.
positions.quote: Digital freedoms, firearm rights, LGBT+ rights, the rights of minorities, the right to abortion, and the right to rural traditions will all be protected under Roy's administration.

positions.summary: Campaign platform page says he supports a public option and an eventual move to universal health care.
positions.quote: Roy supports a public option for those earning less than 100k per year, which could be funded by increased taxes on Vermonts wealthiest residents. Dean supports an eventual move to universal healthcare.

positions.summary: Campaign platform page says he supports a wealth tax and a cap on net worth, and proposes a 2% increase on large corporations.
positions.quote: Dean supports a wealth tax and capping networth to 1 billion dollars in Vermont to make sure that the income gap can be significantly reduced

positions.summary: Campaign platform page says he supports repealing Act 250, which he describes as restricting housing permitting.
positions.quote: Roy supports scraping act 250, the act from the 70s which restricts housing permitting.

positions.summary: Campaign home page says he supports a gradually increased minimum wage.
positions.quote: Dean supports a public option, and later universal healthcare, along with worker rights and gradually increased minimum wage.

candidates.researchNotes: Positions, statements and priorities come from his campaign website (home and platform pages, which were readable when checked in October 2026). Not found: climate, school choice, police funding, tariffs. Guns and immigration-enforcement text is shown as statements because it does not squarely address stricter gun laws or deportations.

statements.quote: Roy promises no new restrictions on any freedoms. Digital freedoms, firearm rights, LGBT+ rights, the rights of minorities, the right to abortion, and the right to rural traditions will all be protected under Roy's administration.
Dean also promises protection from the increasing authoritarian federal government, and from the now highly active Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

researchNotes: Slate matches the Vermont Secretary of State's 2026 general-election qualified-candidate list (Scott R; Janoo DEM/PROG; Goodband Peace and Justice; Roy Freedom and Unity; Judd Independent). Write-ins are noted but not profiled. Running mates do not apply (Vermont elects the governor separately). Ballotpedia was blocked here, so minor-candidate summaries rely on Politics1 and AP coverage.
